newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Jan payrolls swell 271,000.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Jan payrolls swell 271,000.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department reported the economy added 271,000 new jobs in January compared to a revised rise of 261,000 in December.
The unemployment rate, meanwhile, stood at 5.4 percent, up from 5.3 percent in December.
U.S. economists in a Reuters survey had expected payrolls growth of 237,000 and a jobless rate of 5.2 percent.
WALDO BEST, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "It looks like it's going to be a positive (bond) reaction."
Best continued: "Bonds are (looking) at the drastic fall off in hours worked ... This is a sign that the economy might be losing some momentum" in the first quarter.
Best was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

DONALD MAUDE, CHIEF U.S. ECONOMIST, SCOTIA CAPITAL MARKETS: "Very tame average hourly earnings, but it did come on the heels of sharp increases in two consecutive months. We're still running at 3.8 (percent) year-over-year.
"The (payrolls) number was not as much as some people had feared but a little stronger than some people had hoped."

Maude continued: "What I find most striking was the sharp drop in aggregate hours worked. This number bounces around, but it certainly does not point to an exceptionally strong (Gross Domestic Product). The manufacturing hours decline would probably indicate a drop in industrial production.
"I don't think (the report) would reinforce the view of a March (Federal Reserve) tightening, nor would it defuse it."
DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "Obviously the (Treasury) market loves this number ... The earnings number was the key focus here."

Seto went on: "There was strong contention beforehand to downplay any substantial rise in payrolls; a lot of people talked about seasonal factors ... and certainly we are seeing that. The rise in the unemployment rate together with the modest rise in earnings sets the stage for maybe a delayed reaction by the (Federal Reserve), unless some other inflation problems flare up."

HUGH JOHNSON, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER, FIRST ALBANY CORP: "We're seeing a little bit less tightness in the labor market with the unemployment rate rising and then the average hourly earnings number which was up one cent, which is significantly less than anyone expected.

"This pretty much tells you the Federal Reserve will put policy on hold; there's no danger of them raising rates before their next meeting. If you're looking where the employment numbers are going in the future, look at the decline in the average manufacturing workweek, which is a component of the index of Leading Economic Indicators."

DAVID SLOAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, I.D.E.A. INC: "Generally, there were not any huge surprises in the data. The payrolls were a little stronger than expected, and the November jobs number was revised up significantly. The earnings data were reasonably subdued after two strong rises, although the trend is still up. The (Bureau of Labor Statistics) said the workweek was depressed by harsh winter weather.

"The data do not suggest any major change in the picture. They still are suggesting reasonably strong growth in the economy though the inflation pressures, while picking up, are not anything to panic about."
Sloan added: "Hourly earnings maintain the 3.8 percent year-over-year rate, the same pace as December.
"We had two strong months and then one soft month in terms of hourly earnings gains."

SCOTT PARDEE, SENIOR ADVISOR, YAMAICHI INTERNATIONAL (AMERICA) INC: "It is good news for the economy. The (Treasury) market is trading up because there are no signs that suggest the Fed should tighten. Average hourly earnings were up a penny, which shows no sign of inflation coming out of that. And the fact the workweek was down is bullish."

CHRIS IGGO, CHIEF-ECONOMIST, BZW SECURITIES INC: "The headline number was in line with expectations, but we still think it's quite a strong number. Details of the report indicate a fairly tight labor market ... actually job growth was very strong. So, we're a little bit skeptical about how far the (Treasury) market can rally.

"The hourly earnings gave the market a bit for the near term ... that's why the market is rallying at the moment. But this doesn't change our view. We feel the economy is strong and labor markets tight and the Fed will have to tighten."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660 ))
